newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Tajik rebel leader meets Taleban chief in Kandahar.
newsitem.headline: Tajik rebel leader meets Taleban chief in Kandahar.

text.p: Tajik Islamic rebel leader Sayed Abdullo Nuri met the chief of the Afghan Taleban movement in the southern Afghan city of Kandahar on Sunday after the Taleban forced down the U.N. plane on which Nuri was a passenger.

Mullah Abdul Jalil, the Taleban's acting deputy foreign minister, told an Afghan news service that Nuri had had a "good" meeting with Mullah Mohammed Omar, supreme leader of the radical Islamic Taleban movement, who is based in Kandahar.
He gave no details, but stressed that Nuri had visited Kandahar at the invitation of the Taleban and that he and his four Tajik companions were free to go wherever they wished.
"There is no problem at all," Jalil told the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press.
Taleban jets forced Nuri's plane to land at the Soviet-built airbase of Shindand in western Afghanistan on Saturday, saying it had not been authorised to use Afghan airspace.

Diplomats in Islamabad said the Taleban commander of Shindand airbase, about 120 km (75 miles) south of Herat, may have believed that the U.N. plane was carrying ousted Afghan president Burhanuddin Rabbani.
Nuri was on his way from the eastern Iranian city of Mashhad to Kunduz in northern Afghanistan for peace talks with President Imomali Rakhmonov of Tajikistan at an undisclosed location.

After spending a night at Shindand, he flew to Kandahar in a Taleban aircraft. The U.N. plane, a 10-seater Beechcraft, also flew to Kandahar after being released, but developed a technical fault that grounded it there, U.N. officials said.

Alfredo Witschi-Cestari, coordinator of the U.N. Office for Humanitarian Assistance to Afghanistan, told Reuters a second plane would be sent to Kandahar on Monday to fly Nuri's party to Kunduz and a technician would be sent to repair the other one.
The original flight had been requested by U.N. officials in Dushanbe, the capital of Tajikistan.
"We have released the plane and authorised it to fly because it is now clear that it is a U.N. plane," said a spokesman for the Taleban governor of Herat, Mullah Yar Mohammad, earlier.
"We respect the United Nations, but we request that we should be notified about any future U.N. flight," he said.
The United Nations is trying to mediate between the Islamic opposition guerrillas and Rakhmonov's Russian-backed government.
The rebels clashed with government troops in Tajikistan on Sunday only a day before the planned peace talks in neighbouring Afghanistan, Russia's Interfax news agency said.
But the government said on Sunday that talks with Nuri would still take place. "Rakhmonov will go to Afghanistan tomorrow" Tajik presidential spokesman Zafar Saidov said on Sunday.
The Tajik government says the Islamic rebels operate from bases in northern Afghanistan. The Taleban have criticised Tajikistan in the past for alleged meddling in Afghan affairs.

Tens of thousands have been killed and many more made homeless in Tajikistan's bloody four-year civi war where seething regional and clan rivalries underly the conflict between the Islamist rebels and the secular government.
A United Nations-sponsored ceasefire confirmed last July is routinely flouted.
